newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Norway's Orkla sees profit jump 29 percent.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norway's Orkla sees profit jump 29 percent.

text.p: Norway's food-based conglomerate Orkla ASA said on Friday that gains in branded goods and its investment portfolio boosted 1996 pre-tax profits by 29 percent.

The company, which dominates the Nordic branded goods market, also said it was taking over the 52-percent stake held by Swedish carmaker AB Volvo in jointly-owned beverages company Pripps-Ringnes as part of a strategy to grow its business in eastern Europe.

Orkla's group pre-tax profits jumped to 2.43 billion crowns ($363.5 million) from 1.90 billion while earnings per share rose 22 percent to 36.50 crowns. The board proposed to raise the dividend to seven crowns from six crowns.

Group operating revenues increased by four billion crowns to about 26 billion. Operating profits rose to 1.92 billion crowns from 1.80 billion. Net profits came to 1.75 billion, up from 1.43 billion in 1995.
"This increase in profits is attributable to the positive performance of both the Financial Investments and the Branded Consumer Goods areas," a statement said.

In 1996, Orkla's share portfolio achieved a return of 32.5 percent --- 0.4 percentage points better than the Oslo Stock Exchange's All-Share Index. Realised portfolio gains increased by 335 million crowns to 816 million.
For Branded Consumer Goods, operating profits grew to 1.51 billion crowns from 1.13 billion.
The chemicals division's operating profits fell to 441 million crowns from 543 million, partly because of lower speciality pulp prices.

The group's Branded Consumer Goods business in the Nordic markets was likely to maintain its current performance, but growth was expected in eastern Europe thanks to the deal with Volvo on Pripps-Ringnes.

The unit comprises Pripps in Sweden, Ringnes in Norway and 50-percent owned Baltic Beverages Holding (BBH), which has seven breweries in the Baltic States, Russia and Ukraine. In addition, Pripps-Ringnes owns 20.5 percent of the Finnish brewery Hartwall, the other owner of BBH.
Volvo's interest in the jointly-owned firm was valued at 4.0 billion Norwegian crowns. In Stockholm, Volvo said the sale would give the group a profit of 3.0 billion Swedish crowns.

"This takeover sounds very good," one analyst said. "But Orkla already had industrial control of Pripps-Ringnes so they are putting in more money than they needed to. However, the point is that they say they will now be better positioned for growth in Eastern Europe.

"Orkla may form joint ventures with other companies, perhaps already this year. Maybe they'll take over Hartwall. This a confirmation of what Orkla has done for 50 years, namely investing in areas where there is still structural profit to be had."
Orkla took over the Volvo food companies Procordia Food and Abba Seafood in 1995. Pripps and Ringnes also merged to become Pripps-Ringnes, in which Orkla has up to now had a 45-percent interest.

"The Nordic countries are the natural home market for Orkla's branded products," Orkla said. "Outside the Nordic countries, the strongest growth will mainly be in niche areas or special geographical areas.

"Eastern Europe is one such area where Orkla has been working on several fronts for some time. The full takeover of Pripps-Ringnes confirms Orkla's position in the Nordic region and gives the group a strong position in eastern Europe." ($ = 6.684 Norwegian Crowns)
